reconcile.connective: Defenders read the restriction and the Great Commission as one mission in stages — Israel first, then all nations after the resurrection.

discrepancy.connective: D. F. Strauss argued the universal command looks unhistorical: had the risen Jesus ordered a mission to all nations, the disciples would not have needed Acts' vision to admit Gentiles.

skeptic.name: David Friedrich Strauss
skeptic.work: The Life of Jesus Critically Examined (§68)
skeptic.attribution: David Friedrich Strauss (d. 1874), The Life of Jesus Critically Examined, §68 (1835; Eng. tr. 1846)

excerpts.author: Matthew Henry
excerpts.attribution: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14)
excerpts.excerpt_text: This restraint was upon them only in their first mission, afterwards they were appointed to go into all the world, and teach all nations.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly harmonizes the two poles by making the restriction temporary (the first mission) and the universal commission its later supersession — names both poles in one sentence, the squarest answer to the tension.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats the Israel-restriction versus universal-commission tension directly, arguing the particular mission was the appointed first stage of a plan always meant to reach all nations.

link.title: Defending Inerrancy: Is there a Bible contradiction in Matthew 10:5-6?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment harmonizing Matt 10:5-6 with the Great Commission by distinguishing the pre- and post-resurrection mission periods.
